subtitle: Practice moving shared work forward when the people involved do not report to you. You will map who decides and who is affected, share credit fairly, make a case people can act on and handle disagreement with respect.
audience: For program leads, policy leads, project leads and anyone who moves work forward through people who do not report to them, in disability services or across the agency. It also suits people exploring leadership before they hold a title.

lessons.title: Knowing who decides and who is affected
objectives: Identify the decision owner, the people with a stake and the people most affected before you propose a change.
Distinguish the formal authority you were given from the personal authority you bring to a role.
Explain how the order in which you seek agreement shapes whose views count.
Draft a short map of a proposal you lead, including who is rarely asked and how you will reach them.
lessons.teaching:
Influence starts with knowing where the decision sits. Before you propose a change, find out who actually decides, who has a stake in the outcome and who will live with the result. These are often three different groups. A program lead may coordinate a waiver policy update while the decision belongs to a director, the work is done by county and lead agency staff, and the effects land on people receiving services and their families. Kathleen Pogue White's Person-Role-System briefing note, published by the Annie E. Casey Foundation, defines authority simply as the right to do work. It says that stepping fully into your role takes a clarifying conversation with whoever authorized you. Use that conversation to learn what you may decide and what you may only recommend.

Your authority comes in two forms. White separates formal or delegated authority, which is passed to you by someone with more authority, from personal authority, which is the way you take up and carry out that role. She notes that personal authority is shaped by personality, culture and preference. That is worth noticing in yourself. Your habits about when to speak, how hard to push and whom to ask first were learned somewhere. They are one reasonable way to lead, not the only one.

Order matters as much as reach. Most of us seek agreement first from people we already know, people with the most power and people easiest to reach. By the time anyone else hears the idea, its shape is set and their role is to react. The Casey Foundation's Race Equity and Inclusion Action Guide makes a similar point: it is harder to bring new people in once an agenda, strategy and leadership are in place. The guide also separates engagement, which may only mean gathering input, from empowerment, where people help lead, decide and design. Ask early who is most affected and who is rarely asked, and be honest about which kind of involvement you can offer.

A simple map makes the picture visible. Minnesota's Equity Analysis Toolkit asks which groups a proposal is likely to affect, positively or negatively, and names equity and inclusion practitioners, HR leaders and accessibility coordinators among the partners to involve. Use those prompts. Write down the decision owner and what they need to decide. Add the people with a stake. Then add the people most affected, what you know about their experience and how you know it. Where you are unsure, say so and find out. The map is about roles and groups, not notes on individuals.
lessons.keyPoint: Before you propose a change, know who decides, who has a stake and who lives with the result. Bring in the people most affected early, while their views can still shape the idea.
lessons.example: Practice case: Diane is a policy lead asked to simplify renewal paperwork for a disability waiver program. Her draft is ready. She plans to share it with her director, then with two county lead agency supervisors she trusts, then post it for comment. Luis, a self-advocate on an advisory group, tells her that people receiving services usually learn about paperwork changes when the new forms arrive in the mail. Her director wants a recommendation in three weeks.
lessons.question: What should Diane do next?
choices: Keep her plan, since the director decides and the comment period will give people receiving services a chance to respond to the draft.
Confirm with her director what she may change, then invite self-advocates and families to review the draft now, alongside the county supervisors.
Set the draft aside and ask the advisory group to rewrite the paperwork from the start, so that the people most affected lead the change.
feedback: The director does decide, but a comment period on a finished draft asks people to react rather than shape it. The people who fill out the forms are heard last, when changes are hardest to make.
This is the strongest choice. Diane clarifies her authority first, then brings in the people most affected while the draft can still change, and offers a role she can keep.

Inviting affected people to lead has real value, but promising a full rewrite may go beyond what Diane is authorized to do and miss the deadline. Clarifying the boundary first lets her offer a real role.
lessons.reflection: When you last proposed a change, whose agreement did you seek first and whose last? What did that order make easier, and for whom?
lessons.action: Choose one piece of work you are moving forward. Write down who decides, who has a stake and who is most affected. Note one group you have not yet heard from and one way you could reach them this month.

check.question: Your draft is nearly final. You plan to post it so the people most affected can comment. What does that usually offer them?
check.correct: A chance to react to an idea whose shape is already set, not to help shape it.
wrong: A role in leading and designing the change, since their comments can still alter it.
The same influence as the decision owner, since every comment is weighed equally.
check.feedback: Once an agenda and a draft are set, comments mostly react to it. That is engagement. Helping to lead, decide and design needs an invitation while the idea can still change.

lessons.title: Building trust and sharing credit across teams
objectives: Describe how reliability and fair credit build the trust that lets you lead without a title.
Identify moments in meetings and written work where the source of an idea gets lost.
Practice naming the source of an idea when you summarize, report or present shared work.
Plan one change to how your summaries and briefings attribute ideas to the people and teams who raised them.
lessons.teaching:
Without a title, trust is the main thing you have to work with. People on other teams give time to work they do not have to do. They are more likely to do it again when you are reliable: you follow through on what you said, you tell people early when something slips, and you let them know what happened with their input. Reliability sounds ordinary, but the rest of this course rests on it. A program lead who keeps small promises can ask for larger ones.

Credit is part of trust, and it is not always shared evenly. In shared work, ideas travel. Someone raises a point in a small meeting, a colleague repeats it in a larger one, and by the time it reaches a summary or a briefing, the source is gone. The person who first raised it may be newer, quieter, joining by phone, thinking in a second language or simply not in the room. When this happens again and again to the same people, they stop offering ideas, and the work loses what they know. No one has to intend it for the pattern to take hold.

Fair credit is a fairness practice, not a courtesy. Deloitte's report on the six signature traits of inclusive leadership describes fairness in three parts: fair outcomes, fair processes and clear communication with the people affected. It also describes inclusive leaders bringing every team member into discussion and asking follow-up questions. The report is consulting research built on interviews and a small pilot, not a controlled study, but the practice it points to is useful. For credit, a fair process means naming where an idea came from at the moment it is used.

Amplifying an overlooked contribution is a skill you can practice in any role. When a point is passed over, return to it and name who raised it. When you write a summary, attribute ideas to the people or teams who offered them. When you brief a leader, say whose analysis it was, and invite that person to present when you can. Ask yourself whose ideas get credited in your project and how you would know. Then look at your own last few documents. You do not need to keep a tally on anyone to see the pattern; your summaries will usually show it.
lessons.keyPoint: Trust across teams is built from kept promises and accurate credit. Name where an idea came from at the moment you use it, in the meeting, the notes and the briefing.
lessons.example: Practice case: Farah leads a project to speed up interpreter requests across three teams in a human services agency. In an early working session, Oluwaseun, a program consultant who joins by phone, suggested routing all requests through one shared calendar. Two weeks later, a manager from another team presented the same idea at the steering meeting as his team's proposal, and leaders liked it. Farah is now writing the project summary for the deputy director.
lessons.question: How should Farah handle the summary?
choices: Write the summary around the proposal and leave all names out, since what matters most to the deputy director is that the idea moves forward.
Speak privately with the manager about what happened and ask him to correct the record with leaders before she sends anything.
Tell the manager how she will describe the idea, then note in the summary that it came from Oluwaseun's session and thank his team for advancing it.
feedback: Leaving names out feels neutral, but it lets the most recent speaker keep the credit. Oluwaseun's work stays invisible, and others on the project notice whose ideas disappear.
A private word may help later, but it puts the fix on someone else and delays an accurate record. Farah controls her own summary and can make it accurate now without blaming anyone.
This is the strongest choice. Farah makes the record accurate without surprising anyone, gives Oluwaseun visible credit and recognizes the other team's support without assuming harm.
lessons.reflection: Think of a time your idea was credited to someone else, or the reverse. What made it happen, and what would have kept the record accurate?
lessons.action: Look at the last two summaries, notes or briefings you wrote for shared work. Check whether each key idea is credited to the person or team who raised it, and add that attribution to the next one you write.

check.question: Which practice best reflects fair credit in shared work?
check.correct: Naming who raised an idea at the point it is used, in meetings, notes and briefings.
wrong: Leaving every name out of summaries so that no one person gets more credit than another.
Thanking everyone on the project equally at the end, once the final decision is made.
check.feedback: Fair process means credit travels with the idea. Leaving names out or thanking everyone at the end sounds even-handed, but it lets credit settle with whoever spoke last or loudest.

lessons.title: Making a case that people can act on
objectives: Build a case for a proposal around shared values, the problem, its cause, the solution and the action needed.
Adapt the same case for audiences with different responsibilities and concerns.
Offer more than one way for people to respond, so support does not depend on speaking up in one meeting.
Compare how a habit of making a case looks at three points on the intercultural development continuum.
lessons.teaching:
A good case tells people what to do, not only what to think. The Casey Foundation's Race Equity and Inclusion Action Guide describes a framing sequence: the shared values at stake, the problem, its cause, the solution and the action needed. It was written for conversations about race equity, and the sequence also helps with any proposal you lead without authority. A director may need the decision and its risks. A lead agency partner may need to know what changes in their workload. A provider may need the timeline. A self-advocate may want to know what improves for people and how to shape it. The values and facts stay the same; the emphasis changes.

Offer more than one way to take part. A proposal that can only be supported or challenged out loud, in one meeting, favors people who are comfortable speaking quickly in a group. Share material ahead of time in plain language and accessible formats. Invite written comments, short one-on-one conversations and small group discussions as well as the meeting itself. Give people time to check with their own teams. Then check whether it worked: who responded, through which route, and who has not responded at all.

Communication styles differ, and silence is not the same as agreement. People and teams vary in how directly they disagree, whether they raise concerns in public or in private, how much context they expect before a request and how long they need to consult before they commit. Minnesota's Equity Analysis Toolkit describes intercultural competence as being able to see from another cultural point of view and change how you act to fit both differences and what people share. Deloitte's report describes a similar habit in inclusive leaders: changing style when the situation calls for it while staying authentic.

The intercultural development continuum helps you see this skill as a practice that grows. IDI, LLC describes five orientations on its Intercultural Development Continuum: Denial, Polarization, Minimization, Acceptance and Adaptation. A Minimization habit sounds like this: I present every proposal the same way, because a good case speaks for itself. An Acceptance habit notices that people respond differently and that a quiet room may hold real doubts. An Adaptation habit changes the process, for example by sending a plain summary first, holding follow-up conversations and inviting written concerns. These describe habits, not people. Ask which habits shape your own way of making a case.
lessons.keyPoint: Frame the case around shared values, the problem, its cause, the solution and the action needed. Then offer several ways to respond, because a quiet room is not the same as agreement.
lessons.example: Practice case: Yuki is a program lead in disability services who uses live captions in meetings. She is proposing a shared checklist that licensing staff and providers would use before site visits. At a large provider meeting, the licensing manager supports it, but most provider representatives say nothing. Afterward, Greg, who runs two small group homes, emails her that smaller agencies have concerns they did not want to raise in front of the licensing team.
lessons.question: What should Yuki do next?
choices: Send a short plain-language summary, offer brief calls and a written comment option, and share back what she hears before any decision.
Move ahead with the checklist, since the licensing manager supports it and every provider had a fair chance to object during the meeting itself.
Hold a second large meeting and ask each provider in turn to state a view aloud, so that every voice is heard and recorded.
feedback: This is the strongest choice. Yuki adapts the process to how concerns are actually being raised, gives smaller providers routes that feel safe and closes the loop before a decision.
Moving ahead is tempting when the licensing area supports the idea, but silence in front of a regulator may hold real doubts. Concerns that go unheard tend to return later as problems.
Asking each person aloud aims at fairness, but it repeats the setting where people chose not to speak, in front of the licensing team. It may produce answers that are not candid.
lessons.reflection: What do you usually take as a sign that people agree with you? Where did you learn to read agreement that way, and when has it misled you?
lessons.action: Take a proposal you are working on and write it in five short lines: the shared value, the problem, the cause, the solution and the action needed. Then add two ways, besides a meeting, that people could respond.

check.question: Which is an example of an Adaptation habit when you make a case for a proposal?
check.correct: Changing the process, such as sending a plain summary first and inviting written concerns.
wrong: Presenting the case the same way to everyone, because a strong case speaks for itself.
Noticing that people respond differently and that a quiet room may hold real doubts.
check.feedback: Presenting the same way to everyone reflects a Minimization habit. Noticing difference reflects Acceptance. Adaptation goes further and changes how the case is offered so more people can respond. These describe habits, not people.

lessons.title: When agreement does not come
objectives: Plan how to raise an unresolved disagreement with the decision owner without going around anyone.
Distinguish a disagreement about the work from a concern that belongs with Human Resources or the equal opportunity office.
Describe how to carry out a decision you did not want while keeping its reasons visible.
Write a short decision note that records the decision, its reasons and what would prompt a second look.
lessons.teaching:
Disagreement is normal when you lead without a title. People on different teams have different duties, pressures and evidence, and some disagreements cannot be settled by more persuasion. Before you escalate, make sure you understand the other view well enough to state it fairly. Ask what evidence each side has, and what an equity analysis would show about who benefits and who carries the burden. Sometimes the disagreement turns out to rest on a fact you can check together.

Escalate to the decision owner openly, and together where you can. White's Person-Role-System briefing note suggests that when you reach the edge of your authority, the next step is a negotiation with the person who authorized the work, built on the case for what you need. In practice, tell the colleague you disagree with that you plan to bring the question to the decision owner, and invite them to come or to send their view. Try: "We still see this differently. I plan to bring both options to the decision owner this week. Would you like to present yours, or send it with mine?" Present both positions fairly, with the evidence behind each and the effects on the people most affected. Going around a colleague may win once, but it spends trust you will need on the next project.

Some concerns are not disagreements to settle. If what you hear involves possible discrimination, harassment, retaliation, an accommodation, a labor agreement or another personnel matter, it belongs with Human Resources, labor relations or the equal opportunity office, and legal questions belong with counsel. Your role is to help the person reach the right area, not to decide the matter or argue it as part of the project. If you supervise people, ask Human Resources what you are expected to report. Keep it separate from the project disagreement, even when the two feel connected.

Accepting a decision you did not want is part of leading without authority. White describes aligning with others as bearing the loss of sole agency: you contribute to a shared result instead of prevailing. Washington State's enterprise leadership competencies describe public-service leadership in similar terms, including building coalitions and creating enough support to carry out a decision. Once the decision is made, carry it out in good faith and explain it honestly to the people affected. Write down the decision, the reasons and what would prompt a second look. Later, ask what happened, for whom, and what you will keep, change or stop.
lessons.keyPoint: When agreement does not come, take the question to the decision owner openly, with both views stated fairly. Route personnel concerns to the right area. Then carry out the decision in good faith and learn from it.
lessons.example: Practice case: Brian is a project lead redesigning how a human services agency tells people about appointment changes. He wants text reminders paired with phone calls, because older adults and people who use relay services told him texts alone get missed. Valentina, who manages the contact center, wants texts only to control costs and has said she will not change her view. Ifeoma, the deputy director, decides next week.
lessons.question: What should Brian do now?
choices: Let the decision go ahead and raise his concerns afterward if the texts-only approach causes problems, since Valentina's team runs the center.
Tell Valentina he will bring both options to Ifeoma, invite her to present her case alongside his, and share what affected people told him.
Email Ifeoma privately with his evidence before the meeting, so she hears from the people affected before she hears the cost argument.
feedback: Waiting avoids conflict, but it lets the decision go forward without evidence from the people most affected. Raising problems afterward is harder for them and for Brian.
This is the strongest choice. Brian escalates openly, gives Ifeoma both cases and the evidence from people affected, and keeps his working relationship with Valentina intact.
Getting evidence to the decision owner matters, but doing it privately goes around Valentina. Even if it works, it costs trust Brian will need, and Ifeoma hears one side first.
lessons.reflection: Think of a decision at work that you disagreed with. How did you respond once it was made, and what would you keep or change about that next time?
lessons.action: Choose one piece of shared work you move forward. This week, map who decides and who is most affected, check whose ideas your last summary credited, and write how you would bring an open disagreement to the decision owner with both views.

check.question: A project colleague tells you a team member was treated unfairly because of a disability. What is the right next step?
check.correct: Help the colleague reach Human Resources or the equal opportunity office, and keep it apart from the project.
wrong: Raise it with the decision owner as part of the project disagreement, so that it is heard and settled quickly.
Look into what happened yourself first, so you can tell the decision owner whether it holds up.
check.feedback: A concern about possible discrimination is not a project disagreement to settle or investigate. Help the person reach Human Resources or the equal opportunity office, and keep it apart from the project's decisions.

cards.back: The person or area with the authority to make the final call on a proposal. Knowing who it is, and what they need to decide, comes before building support.
Formal authority is delegated by someone with more authority. Personal authority is how you take up and carry out that role, shaped by personality, culture and preference.
Engagement may mean gathering input. Empowerment means people help lead, decide and design. Be honest about which one you are offering before you invite people in.
Returning to an idea that was passed over and naming who raised it, in the meeting, the notes and the briefing, so that credit stays with its source.
Bringing an unresolved disagreement to the decision owner openly, telling the colleague you disagree with, and presenting both views and their evidence fairly.

aid.heading: Before you propose a change
items: Confirm with whoever authorized the work what you may decide and what you may only recommend.
Write down the decision owner, the people with a stake and the people most affected.
Name who is rarely asked, what you know of their experience and how you will reach them early.
Decide honestly whether you are offering a chance to give input or a role in shaping the result.

aid.heading: While you build support
items: Keep small promises, and say early when something will slip.
Credit ideas to the person or team who raised them, in meetings, notes and briefings.
Frame the case: shared values, the problem, its cause, the solution and the action needed.
Offer written, one-on-one and small group ways to respond as well as the meeting.
Check who responded, through which route, and who has not responded at all.

aid.heading: When agreement does not come
items: State the other view fairly, and look for facts you could check together.
Tell the colleague you disagree with that you will bring both views to the decision owner.
Try: "We still see this differently. I will bring both options to the decision owner this week. Will you present yours, or send it with mine?"
Route discrimination, accommodation, labor agreement and personnel concerns to Human Resources, labor relations or the equal opportunity office.
Carry out the decision in good faith and explain it honestly to the people affected.
Later, ask what happened, for whom, and what you will keep, change or stop.

sources.title: Kathleen Pogue White — Person Role System Framework Briefing Note (2013), hosted by the Annie E. Casey Foundation
sources.note: Supports authority as the right to do work, formal versus personal authority shaped by culture, the clarifying conversation and negotiation at the edge of authority, and bearing the loss of sole agency. A consultant's framework for results-based leadership work, not a research study.

sources.title: Annie E. Casey Foundation — Race Equity and Inclusion Action Guide: Embracing Equity, 7 Steps (2014)
sources.note: Supports the points that new people are harder to bring in once an agenda is set, the engagement and empowerment distinction, and the five-part framing sequence. Written for race equity work in 2014; applied here more broadly.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget, Office of Inclusion — State of Minnesota Equity Analysis Toolkit: A Quick Guide (June 2024)
sources.note: Supports the prompt about which groups a proposal may affect, the partners it names, including HR leaders and accessibility coordinators, and its description of intercultural competence. Does not say when use is required.

sources.title: Dillon, B. and Bourke, J. — The six signature traits of inclusive leadership: Thriving in a diverse new world, Deloitte University Press (2016)
sources.note: Supports fairness in outcomes, processes and communication, bringing every team member into discussion, and changing style while staying authentic. 2016 consulting research from interviews in six countries and a small pilot, mostly private sector.

sources.title: IDI, LLC — The Intercultural Development Continuum (IDC)
sources.note: Supports the names and order of the five orientations IDI, LLC describes, used here only to describe habits of making a case at Minimization, Acceptance and Adaptation. Nothing in this course assesses anyone.

sources.title: Washington State Department of Enterprise Services — Washington State Enterprise Leadership Competencies (2025)
sources.note: Supports the description of public-service leadership as building coalitions, managing stakeholder relationships and creating enough support to carry out a decision. Another state's competency model, not Minnesota policy.
